content: The management of breech presentation remains a topic of debate, particularly concerning the use of external cephalic version (ECV) to reposition the fetus. ECV has the potential to decrease the number of breech presentations and reduce the need for caesarean sections. However, there have been reports of complications associated with this procedure. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effects of ECV performed at or near term on various pregnancy outcomes. Methods to facilitate ECV and the use of ECV before term were analyzed separately. The review included randomized trials comparing ECV (with or without the use of tocolytic agents) to no attempt at ECV in women with breech presentation. The authors searched the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Trials Register (as of February 28, 2015) and reviewed reference lists of relevant studies. Two reviewers independently assessed the eligibility and quality of the trials and extracted the data for analysis. Eight studies involving a total of 1,308 women were included in the review. The combined data from these studies demonstrated a statistically significant and clinically meaningful reduction in the likelihood of non-cephalic presentation at birth when ECV was attempted (average risk ratio [RR] 0.42, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.29 to 0.61). Additionally, there was a reduction in the failure to achieve vaginal cephalic birth (average RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.62) and in the rate of caesarean sections (average RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.82). However, the evidence for these outcomes was graded as very low quality. There were no significant differences between the ECV and no-ECV groups in terms of Apgar scores below seven at one minute (average RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.32 to 1.37) or five minutes (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.29 to 1.36), low umbilical vein pH levels (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.17 to 2.44), neonatal admissions (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.34), perinatal death (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.09 to 1.64), or the time from enrollment to delivery (mean difference -0.25 days, 95% CI -2.81 to 2.31). The evidence for these outcomes was also graded as low or very low quality. The trials included in this review had several design limitations. None of the studies blinded the intervention, and the randomization process was suboptimal in several cases. Three of the eight trials had serious methodological flaws. However, excluding these studies in a sensitivity analysis for outcomes with significant heterogeneity did not change the overall results. In conclusion, attempting ECV at term reduces the likelihood of non-cephalic presentation at birth, failure to achieve vaginal cephalic birth, and the need for caesarean sections. However, there is insufficient evidence from randomized trials to evaluate the risks of complications associated with ECV at term. Large observational studies suggest that complications are rare.
